legend: Macroscopic appearance showing a homogeneous tan, fleshy nodular mass lacking a thin fibrous pseudocapsule. Note the peripheral tentacle-like extensions (left) into the surrounding musculature.

Low-power architecture reveals a subcutaneous nodule with subtle peripheral tentacle-like extensions into the surrounding native tissue. Note that this interface may contain chronic inflammation and/or fat necrosis.
Nodular fasciitis infiltrating native skeletal musculature is a common and diagnostically helpful low-power clue.
Longstanding lesions undergo extensive stromal hyalinization and become hypocellular; however, the poorly defined borders with interface inflammation generally remain.

Classic morphology includes loose intersecting fascicles of bland (myo)fibroblastic spindle cells, often with cystic dropout (shown here), with a common finding of pockets of myxoid stroma and extravasated erythrocytes (Fig. <<#55330>>), and at higher-power view, a hypercellular arrangement of bland spindle cells with fine chromatin and tiny, dot-like nucleoli (Fig. <<#55331>>).

Old nodular fasciitis is often hypocellular with stromal hyalinization and may assume stellate cytology.
Nodular fasciitis is characterized by a parallel tram-tracking pattern of SMA immunohistochemistry.

Nodular fasciitis is composed of bland (myo)fibroblastic spindle cells growing in loose fascicles within a variably myxoid stroma. The cells of interest contain fine chromatin with tiny dot-like nucleoli.
